title: Streamer VS (in Development Fighting Game)
author: CryptoCatatonic
selftext:
I've been making a Fighting Game that's completely free to play (and will remain that way) on [itch.io](http://itch.io) I've been trying to hone my skills at game making in general. So I decided to give AI assistance a try to expedite the process. Especially since I want to get feedback to help me improve. And I realized before I concentrated too much on "an interesting idea" or "some cool mechanic" instead of "what makes a game fun and addictive". So I chose to make a fighting game because I was very addicted to these types of games when I was a kid, and want to see why and what ideas I could inject into it through the game maker's perspective.  The current theme is just some silly idea to keep me entertained while working on it.

One of the major goals that I really have for this game is to give the ability of the player to string together their own combos to really allow players to bring their own flair to the way they fight, hence why there is so much fast movement in the game. I was heavily inspired by **Super Street Fighter IV's Juri** and how she used **Feng Shui Engine** to chain together combos in a seemingly limitless way. Which leans into the player being good at the game only if they are keenly aware of their basic moves and placement in the game and capitalizing on opportunities to counter attack. 

the game can be played here, please let me know your thoughts:

[https://mirlygames.itch.io/streamervs](https://mirlygames.itch.io/streamervs)

replies.author: CryptoCatatonic
replies.body: it's been a few months now, with the base sprites being made rapidly it allows me to focus on just making the fighting mechanics work. But also realize there is a connection point with how the game feels when the character moves across the screen with a certain type of responsiveness that is key, so I know I'm going to refine the sprites more to really get that feel in there, whether its the amount of frames or even just where the hitboxes land on the characters, because I realize one real flaw with having sprites generated is that I have to re check them all the time to fit and adhere to the proper dimensions all the time. For some reason AI from chatgpt does not understand or like to adhere to specific sprite sizes and it has a hard time understanding the difference between the size of the image itself and where the character lands inside that image.

replies.author: forgetscode
replies.body:
Few months makes sense. I can tell the amount of polish that went into your work looking at it. Everything looks like it was built with intent.

I have been through your difficulties with sprites. 

I made a rogue lite game with the same approach as you here: https://moosecalibrated.ca/champion-run/

Drift, size, alpha, exposure etc they're very difficult to work through especially with GPT models that are dumb. I have series of auditing procedures but it's mostly a dead end for my standards. Frankly image models are just not designed for making smooth animations.

The approach I tested above in the fighting game I linked was very simple and even half baked(It's a single evening) but if you notice there's a level of smoothness to the animations you can't normally achieve with GPT Claude workflow. The trick I figured out was to use a video model to produce the animations with GPT images as references and anchors and then cut the video into sprite frames.

So what you see in the vid is a cheaper video model(grok imagine 1.0) with opus made references through imagen that was a simple test. 

What I would do next is use grok imagine 1.5, use start and end frames as anchors, describe with intent what I'm trying to achieve and I think that would make the result strong.

Are you interested in working with other people or just trying to keep it solo?
